title: Where? — places and directions
goal: Say where things are with *ở*, use position words like *trên*, *dưới*, *bên cạnh*, *đối diện* — and see that Vietnamese question words stay in place instead of jumping to the front as in English.
bekal: ask where something is with *ở đâu?* and answer correctly
use ten position words: *trên, dưới, trong, ngoài, trước, sau, bên cạnh, giữa, đối diện, gần*
name the important places in a town

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hỏi đường trong khu phố
dialogs.intro: Morning outside the boarding house. Budi needs to send a parcel and get some cash, but doesn't know his new neighborhood yet.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Anh Nam ơi, cho tôi hỏi. Bưu điện ở đâu ạ?
lines.id: Nam, can I ask you something? Where's the post office?
lines.literal: older-brother Nam hey, let I ask. post-office at where (polite)?

lines.text: Bưu điện ở gần chợ, trên đường Lê Lợi.

notes: **Ở does three jobs at once: "at/in", "to be (located)" and "to live".** *Bưu điện **ở** gần chợ* (the post office **is** near the market), *Tôi **ở** Hà Nội* (I **live** in Hà Nội), *Ở trên bàn* (**on** the table). Because it already works as a verb, *Bưu điện ở đâu?* needs no other verb at all — no "is".

**Question words stay where they are.** *Bưu điện ở đâu?* is literally "post office at where?". English moves the question word to the front and flips the verb (*Where is the post office?*); Vietnamese moves nothing. Just put the question word where the answer would go.

**Đâu rồi? is the sentence for something you've lost.** Literally "where already?", it feels like "where's it gone?". With *nhỉ* at the end it becomes a mutter to yourself: *Chìa khoá đâu rồi nhỉ?* — "now where did my keys go?" You'll use it often.

**Ơi is how you call out to someone, and you need it.** *Anh Nam ơi!* = "Hey, Nam!". Calling someone by their name alone sounds hurried and a bit rude; *ơi* softens it. At food stalls and markets it's the first word out of your mouth: *Chị ơi!*, *Em ơi!*

**Khoảng means "about" and goes before the number**: *khoảng mười phút* (about ten minutes). Its partner *thôi* at the end limits it: *khoảng mười phút thôi* = "only about ten minutes" — it's short, don't worry.

**Đúng rồi means "right" or "that's it"**, and it's one of the most useful answers in Vietnamese. Its opposite is *không đúng* or *sai rồi* ("wrong"). If you could keep only three short phrases from this unit, take *đúng rồi*, *ở đâu* and *bao xa*.

grammars.title: Ten position words
body: They are all nouns meaning "top part", "inside", "side", and so on — not prepositions as in English. That's why they're often preceded by *ở* and followed directly by the thing, with no "of" in between.
after: ⚠️ **Bên trái** (left) and **bên phải** (right) use *bên*, meaning "side": *bên trái nhà tôi* = "on the left of my house". You'll use them fully when giving directions in Unit 11.
*Trên* is also used for **street names** — *trên đường Lê Lợi* — just like English "on Lê Lợi Street". For cities and countries, plain *ở* is used: *ở Hà Nội*, *ở Việt Nam*.

grammars.title: Question words stay in place
body: Compare the columns side by side. The Vietnamese and the word-for-word columns have exactly the same order, while normal English moves the question word to the front.
after: ⚠️ **Because question words don't move, don't add *có … không?*.** A sentence that already has *đâu*, *gì*, *ai* or *bao nhiêu* is already a question; adding the Unit 2 frame makes it wrong — like saying "do you go where or not?" in English.

*Bao giờ* has one quirk: **at the start** of the sentence it points to the future (*Bao giờ anh đi?* — when will you go?); **at the end** it points to the past (*Anh đi bao giờ?* — when did you go?). It's the only question word whose position carries meaning.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Nhà vệ sinh* (literally "hygiene house") is the word you'll need soonest and most often forget to practice. The full sentence: *Nhà vệ sinh ở đâu ạ?* Learn it now, not later.

Notice again that almost all of them combine two meaningful words: *bệnh viện* = illness + institute, *sân bay* = yard + fly, *khách sạn* = guest + lodging, *ngân hàng* = silver + shop. Taking them apart makes Vietnamese vocabulary far cheaper to memorize.

blocks.title: Vietnamese addresses run from small to large
items: Addresses are written from **smallest to largest**: *số 25, đường Lê Lợi, quận 1, TP. Hồ Chí Minh* — number 25, Lê Lợi Street, District 1, Hồ Chí Minh City. The order is the same as in English, so nothing needs flipping in your head.

*Số* means "number", *đường* or *phố* means "street", *quận* is an urban "district", *huyện* a rural one. Branching house numbers are written with a slash — *25/3* is read *hai lăm xuyệt ba* — and mean an alley off an alley. In Hà Nội and Sài Gòn this is very common, so don't be surprised if your address has two slashes.
